claim: Breast cancer genomes contain a novel form of mutation showers called kataegis, in which multiple same-strand substitutions at C:G pairs spaced one to several hundred nucleotides apart are clustered over kilobase-sized regions, often associated with sites of DNA rearrangement.
source_text: Breast cancer genomes have revealed a novel form of mutation showers (kataegis) in which multiple same-strand substitutions at C:G pairs spaced one to several hundred nucleotides apart are clustered over kilobase-sized regions, often associated with sites of DNA rearrangement.
evidence_reasoning: This claim references findings from whole genome sequencing of breast cancers, citing prior work (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012).

claim: Kataegis can result from AID/APOBEC-catalysed cytidine deamination in the vicinity of DNA breaks, likely through action on single-stranded DNA exposed during resection.
source_text: We show kataegis can result from AID/APOBEC-catalysed cytidine deamination in the vicinity of DNA breaks, likely through action on single-stranded DNA exposed during resection.
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental data from the yeast model system and inferred from the mechanism of DNA break repair.

claim: Cancer-like kataegis can be recapitulated by expression of AID/APOBEC family deaminases in yeast.
source_text: Cancer-like kataegis can be recapitulated by expression of AID/APOBEC family deaminases in yeast where it largely depends on uracil excision, which generates an abasic site for strand breakage.
evidence_reasoning: This is a primary experimental finding demonstrated through yeast transformation experiments.

claim: Kataegis in yeast expressing AID/APOBEC deaminases largely depends on uracil excision, which generates an abasic site for strand breakage.
source_text: Cancer-like kataegis can be recapitulated by expression of AID/APOBEC family deaminases in yeast where it largely depends on uracil excision, which generates an abasic site for strand breakage.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing reduced kataegis in UNG-deficient yeast.

claim: Localized kataegis can be nucleated by an I-SceI-induced break.
source_text: Localized kataegis can also be nucleated by an I-SceI-induced break.
evidence_reasoning: This is demonstrated through experiments where I-SceI endonuclease was used to induce breaks in yeast.

claim: APOBEC3B and APOBEC3A are the deaminases whose mutational signatures are most similar to those of breast cancer kataegic mutations.
source_text: Genome-wide patterns of APOBEC3-catalyzed deamination in yeast reveal APOBEC3B and 3A as the deaminases whose mutational signatures are most similar to those of breast cancer kataegic mutations.
evidence_reasoning: This is based on comparison of sequence context preferences between yeast mutations and breast cancer mutations.

claim: APOBEC3B and APOBEC3A are implicated in breast cancer hypermutation.
source_text: Together with expression and functional assays, the results implicate APOBEC3B/A in breast cancer hypermutation and give insight into the mechanism of kataegis.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is drawn from mutational signature analysis, expression data, and functional assays.

claim: More than half of 21 sequenced breast cancers contain kataegis.
source_text: Whole genome sequencing of 21 breast cancers recently revealed the presence in more than half the cancers of a novel form of localised hypermutation (termed kataegis)
evidence_reasoning: This references published whole genome sequencing data from Nik-Zainal et al., 2012.

claim: Kataegic mutations in breast cancer occur nearly exclusively at C residues preceded by a 5′-T.
source_text: the fact that the mutations occurred nearly exclusively at C residues preceded by a 5′-T suggested that AID/APOBEC cytidine-DNA deaminases might possibly be involved in the process since these enzymes are sensitive to the 5′-flanking sequence context
evidence_reasoning: This observation comes from analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data.

claim: AID/APOBEC cytidine-DNA deaminases are sensitive to the 5′-flanking sequence context.
source_text: these enzymes are sensitive to the 5′-flanking sequence context (Conticello et al., 2007; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about AID/APOBEC enzymes cited from prior literature.

claim: Members of the AID/APOBEC family of enzymes deaminate cytosine in the context of a single-stranded polynucleotide substrate.
source_text: Members of the AID/APOBEC family of enzymes (reviewed in Conticello et al., 2007) deaminate cytosine in the context of a single-stranded polynucleotide substrate, and function in adaptive and innate immunity.
evidence_reasoning: This is established biochemical knowledge about AID/APOBEC enzymes from the literature.

claim: AID acts on C residues in the DNA of the genomic immunoglobulin loci in activated lymphocytes to trigger antibody gene diversification.
source_text: AID acts on C residues in the DNA of the genomic immunoglobulin loci in activated lymphocytes to trigger antibody gene diversification
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about AID's physiological function.

claim: There are seven APOBEC3 family members in humans.
source_text: APOBEC3 family members, of which there are seven in humans, act on C residues in the DNA of viral replication intermediates (usually in the cytoplasm) as part of a host restriction pathway.
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about the human APOBEC3 family.

claim: APOBEC3 family members act on C residues in the DNA of viral replication intermediates (usually in the cytoplasm) as part of a host restriction pathway.
source_text: APOBEC3 family members, of which there are seven in humans, act on C residues in the DNA of viral replication intermediates (usually in the cytoplasm) as part of a host restriction pathway.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the established physiological function of APOBEC3 proteins.

claim: Off-target deamination by AID results in nucleotide substitutions and genomic rearrangements in B lymphocyte tumours, some of which are implicated in oncogenesis.
source_text: Off-target deamination by AID results in nucleotide substitutions and genomic rearrangements in B lymphocyte tumours, some of which are implicated in oncogenesis (reviewed by Gazumyan et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from the literature about AID's role in B cell tumors.

claim: AID is the only member of the AID/APOBEC family known to act physiologically on endogenous nuclear DNA.
source_text: Although AID is the only member of the AID/APOBEC family known to act physiologically on endogenous nuclear DNA, it is possible that other members of the AID/APOBEC family might occasionally get access to the nucleus and cause cancer-associated genomic damage or mutation
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about the physiological roles of AID/APOBEC family members.

claim: Other members of the AID/APOBEC family might occasionally get access to the nucleus and cause cancer-associated genomic damage or mutation.
source_text: it is possible that other members of the AID/APOBEC family might occasionally get access to the nucleus and cause cancer-associated genomic damage or mutation (Harris et al., 2002; Beale et al., 2004; Vartanian et al., 2008; Stenglein et al., 2010; Landry et al., 2011; Nik-Zainal et al., 2012; Nowarski et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This is a hypothesis supported by various cited studies suggesting potential nuclear access of APOBEC proteins.

claim: All tested members of the AID/APOBEC family expressed in yeast give a significant increase in the mutation frequency as judged by the yield of colonies resistant to canavanine.
source_text: Several members of the AID/APOBEC family members were expressed in yeast and all were found to give a significant increase in the mutation frequency as judged by the yield of colonies resistant to canavanine
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental observation from the canavanine resistance assays.

claim: The median overall intermutational distance (IMD) in AID* yeast transformants is 13 kb.
source_text: While the median overall intermutational distance (IMD) is 13 kb, it is apparent that rather than the mutations being scattered randomly over the genome, mutation distribution is bimodal
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from genome sequencing analysis of yeast transformants.

claim: Mutation distribution in AID* yeast transformants is bimodal rather than random.
source_text: While the median overall intermutational distance (IMD) is 13 kb, it is apparent that rather than the mutations being scattered randomly over the genome, mutation distribution is bimodal
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from statistical analysis of intermutational distances compared to random distribution.

claim: Singlet mutations in AID* yeast transformants exhibit a median IMD of 156 kb with a distribution expected for mutations randomly scattered over the yeast genome.
source_text: Dividing the mutations into two groups using k-means cluster analysis (Hartigan and Wong, 1979) reveals that one group exhibit a median IMD of 156 kb with a distribution of distances that is as expected for a set of individual mutations randomly scattered over the yeast genome as judged by Monte Carlo simulation
evidence_reasoning: This is based on statistical analysis using k-means clustering and Monte Carlo simulation.

claim: Singlet mutations account for 52% of the total mutations in AID* yeast transformants.
source_text: We designate these as singlet mutations: they account for 52% of the total mutations.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative result from the mutation analysis.

claim: Proximal mutations in AID* yeast transformants are separated from each other by a median IMD of only 727 bp with >99% being within 8.5 kb of their closest neighbour.
source_text: The remaining 48% of the mutations are much more closely spaced than would be expected on a random basis. We designate these as proximal mutations, which are separated from each other by a median IMD of only 727 bp with >99% of them being within 8.5 kb of their closest neighbour.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from the mutation distance analysis.

claim: 75% of AID*-induced proximal mutations are found within clusters containing ≥5 proximal mutations.
source_text: Thus, if we define proximal mutations as a pair of mutations that are located <8.5 kb apart (a distance that excludes 99% of the singlet mutations) and define a cluster as a stretch of DNA containing ≥5 proximal mutations, we find that 75% of the AID*-induced proximal mutations are actually parts of clusters.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative result from cluster analysis of the mutation data.

claim: Mutation clusters in AID* yeast transformants typically extend over 6–15 kb with the full range detected being 1.8–30 kb.
source_text: These clusters typically extend over 6–15 kb (with the full range detected being 1.8–30 kb) and contain anything up to 26 mutations
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct measurement from the genomic analysis of mutation clusters.

claim: More than one-third of AID* yeast transformants (16/40) contain at least one mutation cluster.
source_text: The level of mutation clustering observed with AID* is such that more than one-third of the transformants analysed (16/40) contain at least one mutation cluster.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental dataset.

claim: In affected clones, a quarter to two-thirds of all mutations are concentrated in a small number of clusters that account for <0.2% of the entire genome.
source_text: In affected clones, a quarter to two-thirds of all the mutations in the cell are concentrated in a small number of clusters that account for <0.2% of the entire genome.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative analysis of mutation distribution in clustered regions.

claim: Similar mutation clusters are observed in yeast cells transformed with APOBEC3A, APOBEC3B, and APOBEC3G*.
source_text: Similar clusters were also observed in yeast cells transformed with APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B as well as with the hyperactive APOBEC3G mutant APOBEC3G*
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental observation from multiple yeast transformation experiments.

claim: Clustered mutations in yeast transformants show a strong tendency towards strand polarity, with over 88% of mutations being strand coordinated.
source_text: Like the cancer kataegis, the clustered mutations in the various yeast transformants showed a strong tendency towards strand polarity; mutations within a cluster occur predominantly at either a C residue or a G residue with over 88% of mutations being strand coordinated
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from analysis of mutation strand distribution.

claim: 76% of mutations in yeast AID* transformants are C→T transitions.
source_text: Exploring the mutational spectra, we find that the majority (76%) of the mutations in the yeast AID* transformants are C→T transitions
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative result from mutational spectrum analysis.

claim: Transversions are preferentially associated with kataegic stretches in yeast AID* transformants.
source_text: although transversions do occur and these are preferentially associated with the kataegic stretches
evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from comparing mutation types in clustered vs. unclustered regions.

claim: C→T transitions likely arise through direct replication over uracils generated by cytidine deamination.
source_text: Whereas C→T transitions will likely arise through direct replication over uracils generated by cytidine deamination
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from established knowledge about how uracil in DNA leads to C→T transitions during replication.

claim: Transversions are presumably due to replication over abasic sites created through uracil excision by uracil-DNA glycosylase (UNG).
source_text: transversions are presumably due to replication over abasic sites created through uracil excision by uracil-DNA glycosylase (UNG).
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from knowledge of UNG function and the mechanism of translesion synthesis.

claim: Transversions exhibit a strong (4- to 10-fold) bias for C→G rather than C→A substitutions.
source_text: The transversions exhibit a strong (4- to 10-fold) bias for C→G rather than C→A substitutions (Table 1)
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative observation from the mutational spectrum analysis.

claim: REV1 translesion polymerase inserts C opposite abasic sites by virtue of its deoxycytidyl nucleotide transferase activity.
source_text: suggesting that the replication over the abasic site could be catalysed by REV1 since this translesion polymerase (by virtue of its deoxycytidyl nucleotide transferase activity) inserts C opposite abasic sites (Nelson et al., 1996).
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about REV1 function cited from the literature.

claim: Deficiency in either REV1 or UNG leads to a dramatic fall in the proportion of transversion mutations.
source_text: Indeed, deficiency in either REV1 or UNG led to a dramatic fall in the proportion of transversion mutations (Table 1).
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental observation from genetic knockout experiments.

claim: Deficiency in UNG results in a fourfold increase in the average total mutation load in AID* transformants.
source_text: Deficiency in UNG also resulted in a fourfold increase in the average total mutation load in AID* transformants (Supplementary file 1B).
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from comparison of wild-type and UNG-deficient yeast.

claim: The increased mutation load in UNG-deficient yeast reflects diminished repair of AID/APOBEC-generated uracils.
source_text: This presumably reflects diminished repair of the AID/APOBEC-generated uracils.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the known role of UNG in base excision repair of uracil.

claim: There is an overall decrease in average total mutation load in AID* transformants of REV1 deficient yeast.
source_text: There was an overall decrease in average total mutation load in AID* transformants of REV1 deficient yeast that might reflect the possible non-catalytic roles of REV1 during DNA damage repair (Sale et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This is an experimental observation with an inferred explanation based on known REV1 functions.

claim: UNG-deficiency diminishes kataegis in yeast despite increasing overall mutation load.
source_text: We found that the increased mutation load in AID* ung1Δ transformants was accompanied by a dramatic shift away from mutational clustering
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental observation from comparing wild-type and UNG-deficient yeast.

claim: The percentage of proximal mutations falls from 48% in wild type cells to 18% in ung1Δ transformants expressing AID*.
source_text: Despite the fourfold 'increase' in mutation load, the percentage of mutations that are <8.5 kb from their neighbour (proximal mutations) actually 'falls' from accounting for 48% of the AID* mutations in wild type cells to 18% in ung1Δ transformants.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative comparison between wild-type and UNG-deficient yeast.

claim: 274 of 1064 mutations in AID* wild type transformants are found within clusters compared to 28 of 2088 mutations in AID* ung1Δ transformants.
source_text: Similarly, using the same criterion to distinguish clustered mutations in both datasets (≥5 linked mutations separated from their neighbour by <8.5 kb), 274 of the 1064 mutations observed in AID* wild type transformants are found within clusters compared to 28 of the 2088 mutations in the AID* ung1Δ transformants
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative result from cluster analysis of both datasets.

claim: The median overall IMD increases from 13 kb in AID* wild type transformants to 41 kb in ung1Δ cells despite the increase in mutation load.
source_text: Thus, the median overall IMD actually 'increases' from 13 kb in AID* wild type transformants to 41 kb in the ung1Δ cells despite the increase in mutation load.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement comparing intermutational distances in the two genetic backgrounds.

claim: The average number of clustered mutations per yeast transformant is 6.9 in the wild type background vs 1.5 in the ung1Δ transformants.
source_text: There is also an absolute fall in the amount of kataegis as judged by either the average number of clustered mutations per yeast transformant (6.9 in the wild type background vs 1.5 in the ung1Δ transformants)
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative comparison of kataegis frequency between genetic backgrounds.

claim: 26 kataegic stretches were found in 40 AID* transformants in the wild type background vs 4 kataegic stretches in 19 AID* transformants in ung1Δ background.
source_text: or by the frequency of kataegic events (26 kataegic stretches in 40 AID* transformants in the wild type background vs 4 kataegic stretches in 19 AID* transformants in ung1Δ background)
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement of kataegis frequency in the two genetic backgrounds.

claim: Kataegis is substantially reduced but not completely lost in the UNG-deficient background.
source_text: Thus, it is evident that kataegis is substantially reduced in the UNG-deficient background, but not completely lost: a few residual clusters (which exhibit evident strand polarity or bipolarity) are still detected
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations in UNG-deficient yeast.

claim: Kataegis is, at least in part, triggered through the generation of abasic sites.
source_text: The sensitivity of kataegis to UNG-deficiency indicates that kataegis is, at least in part, triggered through the generation of abasic sites.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the experimental observation that UNG deficiency reduces kataegis.

claim: Cleavage at abasic sites by apyrimidinic endonucleases will lead to occasional double-stranded DNA breaks.
source_text: Cleavage at abasic sites by apyrimidinic endonucleases will lead to occasional double-stranded DNA breaks
evidence_reasoning: This is based on established knowledge of how abasic sites are processed in DNA repair.

claim: Kataegis could result from AID/APOBEC deamination of single-stranded DNA exposed during the resection phase of break repair.
source_text: kataegis could result from AID/APOBEC deamination of single-stranded DNA exposed during the resection phase of break repair.
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic hypothesis inferred from the experimental observations.

claim: Co-expression of I-SceI together with APOBEC3G* increases the likelihood of kataegis in the vicinity of the I-SceI cut site.
source_text: Consistent with previous findings (Poltoratsky et al., 2010), induction of I-SceI expression resulted in an increased frequency of deaminase-dependent selectable mutation at the linked CAN1 locus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). More importantly, in the presence of APOBEC3G*, induction of a double-strand break increases the probability that mutations in its vicinity are kataegic
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental observation from the I-SceI break induction experiments.

claim: Induction of I-SceI expression results in an increased frequency of deaminase-dependent selectable mutation at the linked CAN1 locus.
source_text: Consistent with previous findings (Poltoratsky et al., 2010), induction of I-SceI expression resulted in an increased frequency of deaminase-dependent selectable mutation at the linked CAN1 locus
evidence_reasoning: This is an experimental observation consistent with prior published findings.

claim: Most breast cancers identifiable by rainfall plots as harbouring major regions of kataegis also contain clusters comprising smaller numbers of same-strand nucleotide substitutions at 5′-TC dinucleotides.
source_text: Most of the cancers identifiable by rainfall plots as harbouring major regions of kataegis also contain clusters comprising smaller numbers of same-strand nucleotide substitutions at 5′-TC dinucleotides
evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from analysis of breast cancer genome sequencing data.

claim: Over 91% of kataegic C mutations in tumours PD4103a, PD4107a and PD4199a are preceded by a T.
source_text: In tumours PD4103a, PD4107a and PD4199a, over 91% of the kataegic C mutations are preceded by a T
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from sequence context analysis of breast cancer mutations.

claim: Breast cancer kataegic mutations show exceedingly mild sensitivity to the identity of the base at position −2 (average A:C:G:T = 32:20:19:29 compared to human genome average of 30:20:20:30).
source_text: However, any sensitivity to the identity of the base at position −2 is exceedingly mild (average across the kataegic stretches in these three tumours is A:C:G:T = 32:20:19:29 compared to the human genome average of 30:20:20:30)
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative analysis of sequence context preferences in breast cancer mutations.

claim: AID prefers A/G at position −1 relative to the target cytosine.
source_text: Their flanking sequence preferences (reviewed in Conticello et al., 2007) are either radically different (e.g., AID prefers A/G at −1; APOBEC3G prefers C at −1)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about AID sequence preference from the literature.

claim: APOBEC3G prefers C at position −1 relative to the target cytosine.
source_text: Their flanking sequence preferences (reviewed in Conticello et al., 2007) are either radically different (e.g., AID prefers A/G at −1; APOBEC3G prefers C at −1)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about APOBEC3G sequence preference from the literature.

claim: AID has a consensus motif of 5′-WRC (W=A/T, R=A/G).
source_text: With AID, APOBEC3C and APOBEC3G the yeast data essentially confirm the previously identified sensitivity to nucleotides located at positions −1 and −2 (AID: 5′-WRC, APOBEC3C: 5′-TYC, APOBEC3G: 5′-CCC)
evidence_reasoning: This is confirmed by the yeast genome-wide data and consistent with prior knowledge.

claim: APOBEC3C has a consensus motif of 5′-TYC (Y=C/T).
source_text: With AID, APOBEC3C and APOBEC3G the yeast data essentially confirm the previously identified sensitivity to nucleotides located at positions −1 and −2 (AID: 5′-WRC, APOBEC3C: 5′-TYC, APOBEC3G: 5′-CCC)
evidence_reasoning: This is confirmed by the yeast genome-wide data and consistent with prior knowledge.

claim: APOBEC3G has a consensus motif of 5′-CCC.
source_text: With AID, APOBEC3C and APOBEC3G the yeast data essentially confirm the previously identified sensitivity to nucleotides located at positions −1 and −2 (AID: 5′-WRC, APOBEC3C: 5′-TYC, APOBEC3G: 5′-CCC)
evidence_reasoning: This is confirmed by the yeast genome-wide data and consistent with prior knowledge.

claim: Both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B strongly prefer a T at position −1 (91%).
source_text: With regard to APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B, the results reveal that (consistent with earlier studies on APOBEC3B; Bishop et al., 2004), both enzymes strongly prefer a T at position −1 (91%).
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast.

claim: Unlike other deaminases, both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B show mild discrimination with regard to the bases located at position −2.
source_text: However, the yeast studies reveal that unlike other deaminases, both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B show mild discrimination with regard to the bases located at position −2 (APOBEC3A, A:C:G:T = 25:26:7:42; APOBEC3B, A:C:G:T = 35:14:20:31)
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative observation from sequence context analysis in yeast.

claim: APOBEC3A shows position −2 base preference of A:C:G:T = 25:26:7:42.
source_text: both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B show mild discrimination with regard to the bases located at position −2 (APOBEC3A, A:C:G:T = 25:26:7:42; APOBEC3B, A:C:G:T = 35:14:20:31)
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast.

claim: APOBEC3B shows position −2 base preference of A:C:G:T = 35:14:20:31.
source_text: both APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B show mild discrimination with regard to the bases located at position −2 (APOBEC3A, A:C:G:T = 25:26:7:42; APOBEC3B, A:C:G:T = 35:14:20:31)
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative measurement from genome-wide mutation analysis in yeast.

claim: APOBEC3B has a mutational signature that fits extremely well with the kataegis in breast cancer tumours PD4107a and PD4103a (p values <0.005).
source_text: Comparing the contexts of the mutations obtained with the individual deaminases in yeast to those of the kataegic mutations in the cancers reveals that APOBEC3B has a signature that fits extremely well with the kataegis in PD4107a and PD4103a whereas APOBEC3A fits better with PD4199a (p values in all three cases <0.005)
evidence_reasoning: This is based on statistical comparison of sequence context preferences between yeast and cancer mutations.

claim: APOBEC3A has a mutational signature that fits better with the kataegis in breast cancer tumour PD4199a (p value <0.005).
source_text: Comparing the contexts of the mutations obtained with the individual deaminases in yeast to those of the kataegic mutations in the cancers reveals that APOBEC3B has a signature that fits extremely well with the kataegis in PD4107a and PD4103a whereas APOBEC3A fits better with PD4199a (p values in all three cases <0.005)
evidence_reasoning: This is based on statistical comparison of sequence context preferences between yeast and cancer mutations.

claim: A marked bias towards a 5′-T is seen amongst the individual singlet C mutations in several breast tumours (e.g., PD4199a, PD4005a and PD4120a).
source_text: Interestingly, a marked bias towards a 5′-T is also seen amongst the individual singlet C mutations in several of the breast tumours (e.g., PD4199a, PD4005a and PD4120a
evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from sequence context analysis of breast cancer mutations.

claim: APOBEC3A has been shown to be capable of causing genomic damage in mammalian cells.
source_text: Although APOBEC3A has been shown to be capable of causing genomic damage in mammalian cells
evidence_reasoning: This references prior published work on APOBEC3A function in mammalian cells.

claim: Enforced expression of APOBEC3B in KBM7 cells leads to reduced cell viability.
source_text: Stable transfectants of KBM7 cells that inducibly express APOBEC proteins were incubated with inducer (doxycyclin) and viability was monitored after 72 hr.
evidence_reasoning: This is shown in the experimental data (Figure 4A1) demonstrating reduced viability upon APOBEC3B expression.

claim: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B leads to induction of histone γH2AX.
source_text: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B leads to induction of histone γH2AX and of 53BP1 foci.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental observation from flow cytometry and immunofluorescence assays.

claim: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B leads to induction of 53BP1 foci.
source_text: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B leads to induction of histone γH2AX and of 53BP1 foci.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct experimental observation from immunofluorescence microscopy.

claim: APOBEC3B shows the highest and broadest pattern of expression among APOBEC3s in breast cancer cell-lines.
source_text: RNA analysis revealed that although several APOBEC3s can be expressed in individual breast cancer cell-lines, the highest and broadest pattern of expression was evident with APOBEC3B
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from qRT-PCR analysis of breast cancer cell lines.

claim: The expression of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B in some breast cancer cell-lines can be enhanced by treatment with phorbol ester or interferon alpha.
source_text: Consistent with studies in other cell-types (Madsen et al., 1999; Koning et al., 2009; Stenglein et al., 2010), the expression of APOBEC3A and APOBEC3B in some of the breast cancer cell-lines could be enhanced by treatment with phorbol ester or interferon alpha.
evidence_reasoning: This is an experimental observation consistent with prior published findings in other cell types.

claim: The stimulation of local kataegis in yeast by the induction of an I-SceI break indicates that the process occurs during DNA break repair.
source_text: The stimulation of local kataegis in yeast by the induction of an I-SceI break indicates that the process occurs during DNA break repair, most likely by AID/APOBEC-catalysed deamination of cytidines exposed on single-stranded DNA during the resection phase of homology-mediated repair.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the experimental observation that I-SceI breaks stimulate kataegis.

claim: The lengths of the kataegic stretches (mostly in the range 6–15 kb) are in the same order as the extent of resection observed during yeast DNA break repair.
source_text: The lengths of the kataegic stretches (mostly in the range 6–15 kb) are in the same order as the extent of resection observed during yeast DNA break repair (reviewed in Paull, 2010)
evidence_reasoning: This is a comparison between observed kataegis lengths and known resection lengths from the literature.

claim: The distances separating adjacent mutations within yeast kataegic stretches (averaging about 1.2 kb in the AID* dataset) might reflect that the deaminase both jumps and slides on ssDNA, acting with possibly low efficiency at each encountered cytidine.
source_text: The distances separating adjacent mutations within the yeast kataegic stretches (averaging about 1.2 kb in the AID* dataset) might in part reflect that the deaminase both jumps and slides on ssDNA, acting with possibly low efficiency at each encountered cytidine as proposed by Goodman (Chelico et al., 2006).
evidence_reasoning: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the observed mutation spacing based on prior models of deaminase activity.

claim: Residual kataegis observed in the absence of UNG might reflect that breaks will occasionally occur spontaneously through other means.
source_text: That some residual kataegis is still observed in the absence of UNG might well reflect that breaks will occasionally occur spontaneously through other means.
evidence_reasoning: This is a hypothesis to explain the observation of residual kataegis in UNG-deficient cells.

claim: The finding that a double-strand break can be the nucleating lesion for kataegis in yeast is consistent with the close association of kataegis and rearrangements in breast cancer.
source_text: The finding that a double-strand break can be the nucleating lesion for kataegis in this yeast experimental system is consistent with the close association of kataegis and rearrangements in breast cancer (Nik-Zainal et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This connects the experimental yeast findings to observations in breast cancer genomes.

claim: APOBEC-catalysed kataegic deamination in exposed stretches of single-stranded DNA in cancer cells might itself lead to DNA breaks.
source_text: Whereas the yeast data demonstrate that double-strand breaks can nucleate kataegis, it is probable that APOBEC-catalysed kataegic deamination in exposed stretches of single-stranded DNA in the cancer cells might itself lead to DNA breaks.
evidence_reasoning: This is a hypothesis about the bidirectional relationship between breaks and kataegis in cancer.

claim: Recombinational repair of double-strand breaks in yeast is associated with an increased frequency of local mutations with implication of error-prone polymerases.
source_text: It has long been known that recombinational repair of double-strand breaks in yeast is associated with an increased frequency of local mutations with implication of error-prone polymerases (Strathern et al., 1995).
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from prior literature about yeast DNA repair.

claim: The signatures of the mutations associated with the I-SceI break implicate APOBEC3 activity rather than error-prone polymerases as the source of mutations during double-strand break repair.
source_text: In our experiments, the signatures of the mutations associated with the I-SceI break (see Figure 2D legend) implicate APOBEC3 activity rather than error-prone polymerases as the source of mutations during the double-strand break repair.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the sequence context of mutations observed near the I-SceI break site.

claim: Extensive clusters of mutations can be induced in yeast by alkylating agents acting on single-stranded DNA.
source_text: More recently Gordenin and colleagues have shown that extensive clusters of mutations can be induced in yeast by alkylating agents acting on single-stranded DNA (Roberts et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This references recent published work by another group on mutation clustering in yeast.

claim: AID/APOBEC-mediated kataegic hypermutation can be viewed as a specialised example of localised hypermutation caused by exposure of single-stranded DNA during homologous recombination.
source_text: Thus, the AID/APOBEC-mediated kataegic hypermutation, driven by these endogenous mutagens, can be viewed as a specialised, albeit dramatic, example of localised hypermutation caused by exposure of single-stranded DNA during homologous recombination, along the lines proposed by Roberts (Roberts et al., 2012).
evidence_reasoning: This is a conceptual interpretation placing the findings in the context of prior work on localized hypermutation.

claim: Transversions in yeast are specifically associated with kataegic stretches whereas the unclustered mutations in the same cells are restricted to transitions.
source_text: It is striking that transversions in yeast are specifically associated with kataegic stretches whereas the unclustered mutations in the same cells are restricted to transitions.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from comparing mutation types in clustered vs. unclustered regions.

claim: Singlet uracils largely encounter UNG as part of the base-excision repair process (which would be non-mutagenic); the C→T transition mutations would be the result of direct replication over the non-excised uracil.
source_text: The reason for this is a matter for speculation but we suspect the singlet uracils largely encounter UNG as part of the base-excision repair process (which would be non-mutagenic); the C→T transition mutations would be the result of direct replication over the non-excised uracil.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for the observed mutation patterns.

claim: The action of UNG on uracil in a stretch of exposed single-stranded DNA may yield an abasic site that is replicated over by a translesion polymerase rather than repaired.
source_text: In contrast, the action of UNG on uracil in a stretch of exposed single-stranded DNA may yield an abasic site that is replicated over by a translesion polymerase rather than repaired.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative mechanistic explanation for why transversions are enriched in kataegic regions.

claim: Other processes that cause significant exposure of single-stranded DNA (e.g., DNA spooling caused by replication fork stalling; R-loop structures generated during transcription) could predispose to kataegis.
source_text: One can well imagine that other processes that cause significant exposure of single-stranded DNA (e.g., DNA spooling caused by replication fork stalling [Lopes et al., 2006]; R-loop structures generated during transcription of suitable target sequences [Aguilera and Gómez-González, 2008]) could predispose to kataegis.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative hypothesis about alternative mechanisms that could lead to kataegis.

claim: The kataegic stretches in breast cancer display a twofold to fivefold higher average mutation density compared to yeast kataegis.
source_text: Comparison of the yeast and breast cancer data reveals that the kataegic stretches in both sets extend over a similar range of lengths but with the cancer kataegis displaying a twofold to fivefold higher average mutation density.
evidence_reasoning: This is a quantitative comparison between yeast and breast cancer kataegis characteristics.

claim: The higher mutation density in cancer kataegis compared to yeast could reflect differences in deaminase activity in the two organisms.
source_text: This could reflect differences in deaminase activity in the two organisms.
evidence_reasoning: This is a speculative explanation for the observed difference in mutation density.

claim: Cancers which harbour kataegic stretches comprising larger numbers of mutations additionally contain multiple clusters with smaller numbers of T-C mutations.
source_text: It also appears that those cancers which harbour kataegic stretches comprising larger numbers of mutations additionally contain multiple clusters with smaller numbers of T-C mutations
evidence_reasoning: This is an observation from analysis of breast cancer genome data.

claim: The marked bias towards a 5′-T seen amongst some cancer singlet C mutations suggests that kataegis might be signalling a much wider implication of APOBEC-mediated deamination in genome-wide mutagenesis in some tumours.
source_text: The marked bias towards a 5′-T seen amongst some cancer singlet C mutations suggests that kataegis might be signalling a much wider implication of APOBEC-mediated deamination in genome-wide mutagenesis in some tumours.
evidence_reasoning: This is an inference drawn from the observation of TC-biased singlet mutations in some tumors.

claim: The mutation data obtained in yeast reveal APOBEC3B and APOBEC3A as the only deaminases characterised whose target specificity matches the breast cancer kataegic mutations.
source_text: The mutation data obtained in yeast reveal APOBEC3B and APOBEC3A as the only deaminases characterised whose target specificity matches the breast cancer kataegic mutations, arguing very strongly for an involvement of these deaminases in cancer kataegis.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing sequence context preferences across all tested deaminases.

claim: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A (as well as APOBEC3C and 3H) can lead to mutation of human papilloma viral DNA.
source_text: The implication of APOBEC3A fits with data from others revealing that enforced expression of APOBEC3A (as well as APOBEC3C and 3H) can lead to mutation of human papilloma viral DNA (Vartanian et al., 2008)
evidence_reasoning: This references prior published work on APOBEC3A activity on viral DNA.

claim: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A can lead to mutation of transfected plasmid DNA.
source_text: as well as of transfected plasmid DNA (Stenglein et al., 2010)
evidence_reasoning: This references prior published work on APOBEC3A mutagenic activity.

claim: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A has been shown to lead to genomic damage in the nucleus.
source_text: Enforced expression of APOBEC3A has also been shown to lead to genomic damage in the nucleus (Landry et al., 2011).
evidence_reasoning: This references prior published work demonstrating APOBEC3A can cause nuclear DNA damage.

claim: APOBEC3B is well expressed in breast cancer cell lines.
source_text: The target-specificity data implicating APOBEC3B in the breast cancer mutation is not only supported by our demonstration that its enforced expression can yield DNA damage but also by the fact that it is well expressed in breast cancer cell lines.
evidence_reasoning: This is a direct observation from RNA analysis of breast cancer cell lines.

claim: Burns et al. demonstrated that APOBEC3B expression correlates with a T-C mutator phenotype in many primary breast cancer tumours.
source_text: Furthermore, after submission of this manuscript, Burns et al., have demonstrated that APOBEC3B expression also correlates with a T-C mutator phenotype in many primary breast cancer tumours (Burns et al., 2013).
evidence_reasoning: This references work by another group published after manuscript submission.

claim: APOBEC3B and/or APOBEC3A are the deaminases likely responsible for the breast cancer hypermutation.
source_text: Thus, APOBEC3B and/or APOBEC3A are the deaminases likely responsible for the breast cancer hypermutation although it remains possible that other APOBEC3s might contribute to genome mutation in other tumours.
evidence_reasoning: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined evidence of sequence context matching, expression data, and functional assays.

claim: It remains possible that other APOBEC3s might contribute to genome mutation in other tumours.
source_text: Thus, APOBEC3B and/or APOBEC3A are the deaminases likely responsible for the breast cancer hypermutation although it remains possible that other APOBEC3s might contribute to genome mutation in other tumours.

claim: Double strand breaks are a common feature of tumour development.
source_text: With regard specifically to kataegis, given that double strand breaks are a common feature of tumour development, it will obviously be interesting to discover whether whole genome sequencing of other tumour types also reveals evidence of kataegic hypermutation
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: The AID/APOBEC family has undergone considerable expansion in primates.
source_text: and whether, in light of the fact that the AID/APOBEC family has undergone considerable expansion in primates, such kataegic hypermutation might also have contributed more generally to recent genome evolution.

claim: Kataegic hypermutation might have contributed to recent genome evolution in primates.

source_text: Two-thirds of the CAN1 region mutations in the KanMX-ISceIRS cells were transversions.

claim: High-confidence mutations were present in more than 0.5 variant allele fractions but were more frequently present in all reads reporting that genomic position.

claim: K-cluster analysis was used to divide intermutational distances into two groups designated distal and proximal.
source_text: K-cluster analysis (Hartigan and Wong, 1979) was used to divide intermutational distances (IMDs) into two groups, which we designated distal and proximal.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the statistical method used for analyzing mutation distributions.

claim: A cluster was called when a minimum of 5 adjacent mutations were identified each with IMDs below the threshold.
